topic: Change of Basis in Linear Algebra
target_audience: Undergraduate students in Mathematics, Engineering, or Computer Science

outline.topic: Change of Basis in Linear Algebra
outline.target_audience: Undergraduate students in Mathematics, Engineering, or Computer Science

sections.title: Prerequisite & Hook: The 'Same' Vector
sections.content: Define a vector as a geometric arrow (independent of coordinates). Introduce the idea that while the arrow stays the same, the 'language' (basis) used to describe it can change. Use the analogy of describing a location: '3 miles North, 2 miles East' vs. 'GPS coordinates'.
sections.example: A cat sitting on a 2D floor. Describe its position relative to the corner of the room (Basis A) versus relative to the center of the rug (Basis B).

sections.title: Defining Basis Vectors
sections.content: Explain a basis as a coordinate system defined by linearly independent vectors. Visualize standard basis vectors (e.g., î=[1,0], ĵ=[0,1]) and transform them into custom basis vectors (e.g., b1=[1,1], b2=[-1,1]).
sections.example: Animation: Show the grid lines stretching and rotating from the standard square grid to a skewed, tilted grid.

sections.title: The Change-of-Basis Matrix
sections.content: Introduce the transition matrix (P). Explain that P maps coordinates from the 'New' basis back to the 'Standard' basis. Emphasize the formula: [v]standard = P * [v]new. Show this visually by projecting the new vector components onto the standard axes.
sections.example: Robot Arm: Mapping the position of a robot's claw from its own 'hand-centric' coordinate system to the 'room-centric' coordinate system.

sections.title: Step-by-Step Calculation Procedure
sections.content: Provide a clear 3-step algorithm: 1. Identify the 'New' basis vectors. 2. Construct matrix P by placing basis vectors as columns. 3. Multiply P by the coordinates in the new basis to find the standard representation.
sections.example: Given Basis B = {[2,1], [1,2]}, convert the coordinate vector [1,1]_B into standard coordinates: 1*[2,1] + 1*[1,2] = [3,3].

sections.title: Synthesis & Practical Application
sections.content: Summarize that changing bases allows us to simplify complex problems (like diagonalizing matrices). Highlight that the vector 'object' is invariant; only its 'description' changes.
sections.example: Video Game Physics: Moving a character 'forward' relative to the camera's current perspective versus the world's fixed north direction.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite & Hook: The 'Same' Vector
lecture_lines: A vector exists independently of its coordinate description.
Think of an arrow as a geometric object.
Changing basis is changing the language of description.
animations: Show a single vector in a 2D plane labeled #FFFFFF 'V'.
Highlight vector V with a bright yellow flash #FFFF00.
Display grid lines #4A4A4A to imply coordinate system.

storyboard.title: Defining Basis Vectors
lecture_lines: A basis is a system of independent vectors.
Standard basis vectors define our default grid.
Custom basis vectors tilt and stretch the grid.
animations: Show standard basis vectors i^ and j^ #00FF00.
Display new basis vectors b1 and b2 #FF00FF.
Connect origins of both sets of vectors with dashed lines.

storyboard.title: The Change-of-Basis Matrix
lecture_lines: Transition matrix P links different coordinate systems.
P maps new basis back to standard basis.
Standard coordinates equal P times new coordinates.
View vectors as room-centric or claw-centric.
Projection visually maps new components onto standard axes.
animations: Show Matrix P with placeholder entries #FFFFFF.
Animate columns of P moving into place.
Scale P by a scalar value for visual emphasis #00FFFF.

storyboard.title: Step-by-Step Calculation Procedure
lecture_lines: First, identify your new basis vectors.
Second, build matrix P using those vectors.
Third, multiply P by your coordinate vector.
This maps to standard representation efficiently.
Procedure converts any basis to standard coordinates.
animations: Draw a multiplication arrow between P and V.

storyboard.title: Synthesis & Practical Application
lecture_lines: Change of basis simplifies complex linear problems.
Diagonalization becomes easier with the right basis.
The geometric vector object always stays invariant.
animations: Display a complex scene showing both vector systems.
Animate V transforming from original to new basis.
Overlay final result with a celebratory highlight #7FFF00.
